title: 25. Inclusion of a yeast derived product as a natural feed additive in early weaned calves diet: impact on performance and parameters indicating the level of stress.
content:
Abstract
Early weaning in beef cattle, around 60 days of age, is a frequently adopted practice to improve cows’ body condition score and pregnancy rate. However, nutritional management of calves at such early age can become challenging. Dry lot or confined feeding emerges as an alternative when the diet is well balanced, with feed additives playing a key role to improve growth, feed efficiency, stress response, and health. The objective of this work was to evaluate the impact of substituting monensin as feed additive with a natural yeast-derived product (YDP) (Celmanax™; Church & Dwight Co., Inc.; Princeton, NJ) on early weaned calves’ performance and stress response. Thirty-two spring born castrated Hereford male calves were weaned at 71±10 days of age, and 88 ± 12 kg body weight (BW), stratified by BW and randomly assigned to one of two treatments: 1) total mixed ration with 20% of whole oats as fiber source (TMR without long-size fiber) with monensin (0.15 g/h/d) as feed additive (MON; n = 16); and 2) same TMR substituting monensin with a YDP (7 g/h/d) as feed additive, top-dressed (YDP; n = 16). Calves were housed individually in a semi-roofed pen with feed and water troughs, and received their treatments daily for 73 days, including the adaptation period (17d). Feed was offered twice a day, in two equal meals, adjusting the amount offered every two days to ensure ad-libitum intake. Feed intake (DMI, kgDM/d) was measured every day as the difference between offer and refusals; BW was recorded every 14 days without fasting, and feed-to-gain ratio (kgDM:kgBW) was calculated according to feed intake and BW gain during the experimental period. Blood samples were taken twice from the jugular vein, at the beginning (week 2) and at the end (week 8) of the experimental period, for cortisol determination in plasma. During the same weeks, fecal samples were collected in three consecutive days to estimate total tract apparent digestibility, for DM and organic matter (OM), using acid-insoluble ash as an internal marker. Data was analyzed as a completely randomized design. Inclusion of a natural additive (YDP), as monensin substitute, had no negative impact on average daily gain (ADG) or DMI (P ≥ 0.317), achieving similar final body weight (P = 0.78); but resulted in a better stress response or adaptation due to a lower cortisol level at d73 (Table 1). However, feed-to-gain ratio showed a better efficiency towards MON (P = 0.038) along with greater DM and OM digestibility and lesser water intake (P ≤ 0.041) (Table 1). Nevertheless, it is viable to substitute monensin with a natural feed additive (YDP) without affecting early weaned calves’ performance, even when consuming a TMR without long-size fiber in a confined system.
